title: Pericardial effusion
why_this_matters: Pericardial effusion in dogs can compress the heart (tamponade) and cause collapse; in a cardiology referral series about 42% of dogs with effusion had tamponade, and the cause was often neoplasia or severe valve disease [1].

what_changes_from_human.point: In dogs the commonest neoplasms behind effusions needing drainage are hemangiosarcoma and chemodectoma, plus idiopathic pericardial effusion; a collapsed older dog with abdominal distension or dyspnea can have a cardiac cause [2].
Severe degenerative mitral and tricuspid valve disease was an equally common finding as neoplasia (35% vs 36% of 91 dogs) in one referral series [1].

recognition: Common histories: lethargy, dyspnea, anorexia, collapse and abdominal distension [2].
Echocardiography identified effusion in 91 of 5,304 referred dogs (1.7%); 71 were male. Tamponade was present in 38 of 91 (42%) [1].
Tamponade means intrapericardial pressure equals or exceeds right ventricular diastolic filling pressure, lowering cardiac output [2].

management: Pericardiocentesis stabilizes tamponade, relieves right-sided failure and yields fluid for diagnosis [2].
Complications are rare but include cardiac puncture, arrhythmia, and laceration of a tumor or coronary artery causing intrapericardial hemorrhage or sudden death [2].
In 28 echo-guided drainages with a 17G hemodialysis fistula needle, no adverse effects were seen over 48 hours [1].

takeaway: A collapsed dog with distended abdomen or breathing trouble may have fluid around the heart; get to a veterinarian with ultrasound quickly.
